lead: One token travels between processes; holding it is the right to enter the critical section. The token carries the waiting list, so no process needs to know who is queued elsewhere. Some syllabi call this the broadcast algorithm. It fits small clusters, such as one process writing an end-of-day settlement file while others wait. With N processes all busy, one entry costs N messages: N − 1 REQUEST broadcasts plus one token transfer. Ricart–Agrawala costs 2(N − 1) per entry. Idle cost is 0.
prereq: You need 5.1 for REQUEST and REPLY, and Unit 4 for sequence numbers.

blocks.text: Every process keeps RN[1..N]; RN[i] is the largest request number seen from i. The token carries Q, a queue of waiting ids, and LN[1..N]; LN[i] is the latest request number of i already granted. RN is not in the token.

items: Broadcast REQUEST(i, sn) to the other N − 1 processes.
Every receiver sets RN[i] = max(RN[i], sn).

blocks.text: Only the process granted a request writes its own LN entry, at entry to the critical section.
On REQUEST(j, sn) while holding the token: set RN[j] = max(RN[j], sn). If not inside the critical section and RN[j] = LN[j] + 1, send the token to j now; otherwise append j to Q.

items: Holder i: if RN[i] = LN[i] + 1, set LN[i] = RN[i], enter, work, leave.
After leaving, pop head j of Q and send the token to j; if Q is empty, keep the token.
If no own request is pending and Q is nonempty, send the token to the head of Q.

blocks.where: C is messages per entry when all N processes request continuously: N − 1 REQUESTs plus 1 token transfer. C_RA is the same figure for Ricart–Agrawala. Idle cost is 0 messages.

blocks.text: After a crash duplicates the token, mutual exclusion can break two ways: two processes hold copies and enter together, and the same process may be granted twice, because a stale copy has an out-of-date LN that still passes the entry test. Keep the copy with the larger LN; destroy the other, for example by a token sequence number. See 5.3.

figure.caption: All three requests carry sn = 1. P1 passes the token to P2 with Q empty, and each later request arrives while the holder is inside, so it waits in Q until that process leaves. Entry order is P2, P4, P3, and P3 keeps the token at the end.

spec.aria: Messages in time order among P1, P2, P4 and P3: P2, P4 and P3 each broadcast REQUEST with sn = 1; P1 sends the token to P2 with Q empty, P2 queues P4's request and sends the token to P4 on exit, P4 queues P3's request and sends the token to P3 on exit, and P3 keeps the token.

examples.question: P1–P4 share one token. P1 holds it, Q is empty, RN = LN = [0,0,0,0]. P2, P4, P3 request with sn = 1; REQUESTs reach P1 in order P2, P4, P3. P4 reaches P2 while P2 is inside, and P3 reaches P4 while P4 is inside. Give Q, entry order, LN, messages.
steps: P1 gets P2 first: not inside, RN[2] = 1 = LN[2] + 1, so sends the token to P2. Q is empty.
P2 enters, LN[2] = 1. P4's request arrives inside, so Q = [4]. On exit P2 sends to P4, Q empty.
P4 enters, LN[4] = 1. P3's request arrives inside, so Q = [3]. On exit P4 sends to P3, Q empty.
P3 enters, LN[3] = 1. Q empty, so P3 keeps the token. LN = [0,1,1,1].
Messages: 9 + 3 token transfers = 12 = N per entry.
examples.answer: Entry order P2, P4, P3; LN = [0,1,1,1]; 12 messages, N = 4 per entry.
examples.check:
n = 4
requesters = 3
req_msgs = requesters * (n - 1)
token_msgs = requesters
total = req_msgs + token_msgs
print(req_msgs)
print(token_msgs)
print(total)

traps: i sets LN[i] = RN[i] when taking the token, before entering the critical section. Only the granted process writes its own LN entry.
The entry test is RN[i] = LN[i] + 1, not RN[i] ≥ LN[i] or RN[i] = LN[i].
Use RN[i] = max(RN[i], sn), not RN[i] = sn. A delayed smaller value must not overwrite a larger one.
LN records granted requests; RN records requests seen. Examiners ask for both arrays.
A stale second token lets two processes pass their entry tests at the same time.

quiz.q: Name the two fields the token carries.
quiz.a: Queue Q of waiting ids and array LN[1..N] of granted sequence numbers. RN[1..N] is kept at each process, not in the token.

quiz.q: Why does the token carry Q instead of every process keeping its own queue of waiters?
quiz.a: Only the holder decides who is next, so one copy is enough. Otherwise each process must merge N partial queues, and order depends on message arrival at every site.

quiz.q: N = 6 processes all request continuously. Give the messages per entry here and for Ricart–Agrawala.
quiz.a: Here: (6 − 1) + 1 = 6 messages. Ricart–Agrawala: 2(6 − 1) = 10 messages. Saving is 4 messages per entry.

quiz.q: RN = [0,2,1,0], LN = [0,1,1,0] and process 2 holds the token. May it enter, and what changes?
quiz.a: RN[2] = 2 = LN[2] + 1, so yes. It sets LN[2] = 2, then sends the token to the head of Q if Q is nonempty. Process 3 cannot enter: RN[3] = LN[3] = 1.

quiz.q: A REQUEST(i, 5) arrives at a site where RN[i] is already 7. What happens and why is it safe?
quiz.a: max keeps RN[i] = 7, so the delayed REQUEST(i, 5) changes no state and is ignored. It is safe because the entry test always works from the highest request number seen, so an older number can neither create an extra entry nor push LN[i] backwards; grants only move LN[i] forward, one request number at a time.

quiz.q: After a crash two tokens exist. What can go wrong, and what limits the damage?
quiz.a: Two holders can pass their tests and enter together, so mutual exclusion is lost. The same process can also be granted twice from a stale copy, because its LN is behind. Nothing inside the token limits the damage on its own; one of the two tokens must be detected and removed before either is used again.

beyond: Not for the exam. Raymond's tree-based algorithm sends the token along a path to the requester, cutting messages. Self-stabilizing token circulation is studied for wireless and ad hoc networks. Some cluster lock managers still use a single token holder, though most now prefer lease-based locks.
